Dışişleri Bakanı Hakan Fidan, Ankara'da Suriye Dışişleri Bakanı Esad Hasan Şeybani ile ortak basın toplantısı düzenliyor.
Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanı Abdulkadir Uraloğlu, Bakanlıkta HGS'ye ilişkin açıklama yaptı.
Son günlerde otoyol geçiş ücretleri ve HGS noktasında basında ve sosyal medyada bazı konuların gündeme geldiğini ifade eden Uraloğlu, süreci hem Bakanlık hem de Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğü (KGM) olarak yakından takip ettiklerini söyledi.
Uraloğlu, otoyol geçişlerinde HGS etiketi ve plaka olmak üzere iki şekilde tanımlama yapıldığını ve gerekli ücretlendirmelerin de bu tanımlama üzerinden gerçekleştiğini ifade etti.
HGS'si olmadığı durumlarda plaka üzerinden aracın tespit edilebildiğini belirten Uraloğlu, "Eskimiş etiketler ya da kirlenmiş, deforme olmuş plakalar varsa bu noktada bazı zorluklar yaşadığımız da oluyor. Mevcut sistemin yapay zeka destekli algılamasıyla beraber o plakayı tahmin ediyoruz, ona göre işlem yapıyoruz. Eğer burada bir yanılgı var ve bize bildirilmişse geriye doğru yapılmış olan bütün işlemlerin iptal edildiğini özellikle belirtmek isterim." dedi.
Bakan Uraloğlu, ihlalli geçiş söz konusu olduğunda 15 gün içinde vatandaşlara sisteme kayıtlı olan telefon numaraları üzerinden SMS ile bildirim yapıldığını, bunun bakiyenin yetersiz olması durumunda da gerçekleştiğini söyledi.
Vatandaşlara, tanımlı plakaya ait telefon numaralarını e-Devlet veya HGS sistemleri üzerinden güncelleme çağrısı yapan Uraloğlu, sözlerine şöyle devam etti:
"Biz 15 gün içinde gerekli bildirimi yaptık, eğer vatandaşımızın eksik bakiyesi varsa veya plakası hiç HGS abonesi olmamışsa, 'süre geçti, sen geçemezsin' demiyoruz. 15 gün içinde bir HGS hesabı açar öderse yine hiçbir problem yok. Bunlar olmadı, 15. günden 45. güne kadar bir kat ceza uygulamasıyla yine aynı süreç devam ediyor. Yani vatandaşımız 45. güne kadar eğer öderse bir kat ceza uygulaması söz konusu. 46. günden sonra özellikle kamu-özel işbirliği otoyollarında vatandaşa en az 15 gün içinde bir tebligatla bildirim yaparak bu süreci yine durdurmayı maksatlıyoruz. Eğer bu tebligata rağmen bir işlem, bir ödeme, bir başvuru yapılmamışsa bu sefer olay esasında bizim de istemediğimiz avukatla takip sürecine kadar gidiyor. Burada ben özellikle söylemek istiyorum, bütün bu dediklerim yapılmış da vatandaşa yine bir şekliyle gitmişse biz de birebir takip ediyoruz ve bu sefer ilgili işletmeciye idari yaptırımlar uygulama noktasında da tasarrufta bulunuyoruz. Dolayısıyla bizim vatandaşımızdan beklediğimiz, otoyoldan geçtiğini, hesap bakiyesini bilmesi ama bunlar yoksa bizim bildirimlerimiz üzerine mutlaka gereğini yapması. Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time
Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.
A late and surprise choice, Diallo said, "I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he had the credibility and unifying potential to be able to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.
"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.
"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).
However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.
Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team
While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer", he admitted.
Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.
Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."
They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.
Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."
McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.
"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."
Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.
As recently as August it all seemed very different when the heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered some setbacks.
Uefa called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, and then potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.
Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by £2.6 billion.
Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.
"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.
"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."
"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."
So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?
Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.
The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.
There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.
The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give …

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley , prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027 . Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative .
Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape .

Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for ‘protecting the two-state solution’.
The government of the United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and a settler group blocking aid to Gaza.
The companies affected in Tuesday’s asset freezes include Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd and SAG (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which construct and develop homes in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The measures were announced shortly before the final deadlines for the tenders for E1, a settlement project that would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from occupied East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of an independent state.
“Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this Government’s approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement. “That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”
The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks from delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.
Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull said the sanctions on Tzav 9 come after the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office has noted that thousands of families in Gaza are in dire need of aid after “catastrophic” floods .
Britain’s relationship with Israel has deteriorated significantly over the past three years because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as well as the Israeli government’s plans to expand settlements in the West Bank.
Israel in September threatened to close the British consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.
British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure.
Meanwhile on Tuesday, Israeli forces carried out a series of raids and arrests in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
A Palestinian woman was killed in an attack on Monday night by Israeli settlers firing live ammunition at Palestinians in the area of the village of Ein ad-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho governorate, according to medical sources.
The Jericho Governmental Hospital reported that 10 Palestinians were injured by the settlers’ gunfire, including an elderly man.
Israeli soldiers also raided the Jalazone refugee camp and arrested two people in addition to arresting another person from el-Bireh after searching a home.
Troops also stormed Nablus, Tubas and the villages of Khallet al-Louza and Beit Falouh in Bethlehem governorate, raiding homes and shops and firing tear gas.

Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summit
Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “No 1 terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost of living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon and public holidays put in place for the Asean summit.
After departing from Fairbanks in Alaska, Trump emerged from Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International airport at 5.54pm local time (0954 GMT), live video showed.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen in China on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ousting of the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said. “Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So, yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 100km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 26 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty International said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” Amnesty’s director for the Philippines, Ritz Lee Santos III, said. “Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received ‘spontaneous signs of strong support’ against Infantino.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo says he has the backing of countries beyond Europe in his bid to depose Gianni Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election.
“To beat him you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” Diallo said on Tuesday following his nomination as the European governing body UEFA’s representative.
“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”
Diallo was speaking in Paris the day after accepting an invitation from UEFA to stand against Infantino in the election to be held next March.
UEFA, which has 55 member associations, said that European nations had “unanimously pledged their full support” to Diallo, ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for candidates to declare themselves.
Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was revealed in July.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the current FIFA president in Switzerland.
Diallo announced in September that the French Football Federation (FFF) was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.
“There can no longer be a type of single-handed governance where the biggest issues in football are decided behind the scenes, without any transparency and without anyone being consulted, without going through the executive committee,” Diallo, 63, said on Tuesday.
“My vision will be one of open, collegiate governance, in which the different bodies really play their part.”
Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023.
UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.
Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe’s backing, but he will not stand.
FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election. A majority is needed for a candidate to win.

China said on Tuesday it has "no information" on whether US President Donald Trump would meet Kim Jong-un, after the US president left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader on his Asia trip.
"I have no information regarding this matter," foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a news briefing in Beijing, a day before Trump was expected in Shenzhen for an APEC meeting.
Before departing for China, Trump, who met Kim three times during his first term, left open the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good," Trump told reporters, adding that whether Kim would make the trip was "up to President Xi" of China.
As Trump made the remarks, North Korean state media reported that Kim and his family, accompanied by party officials, travelled to a tourist zone near the northern border with China on Sunday and Monday.
Photos released by the official Korean Central News Agency show Kim sitting on an armchair, grinning, with a cigarette in his hand and sunglasses on, at what appeared to be a ski resort, with his wife Ri Sol Ju standing behind him.
Another photo shows his young daughter Ju Ae, whom Seoul's spy agency has said is being groomed to be Kim's successor, skiing downhill in a white outfit but without a helmet.
The city of Samjiyon is located near the Chinese border and is close to Mount Paektu, considered by North Koreans to be the sacred birthplace of Kim's father, Jong-il.
As he toured the resort, including ski centres and hotels, Kim "expressed great satisfaction, saying that all the structures are really impeccable as they were built in a delicate way", KCNA reported.
"The more he looked at it, the more admiration he felt at the spectacular scenery reminiscent of a town in the forest," it said.
While Kim made the visit near China, which is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, experts say it was unlikely intended to signal plans to travel to the summit.
The straight-line distance between the two cities is more than 2,500 kilometres (1,553 miles).
"The KCNA report does not contain any message aimed at the United States and there are no signs of preparations for a meeting," Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told the AFP news agency.
"Kim's visit therefore is hard to be seen as a preparation for any North Korea-US meeting this week," he said.
Trump and Kim met in Singapore in June 2018, then in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the Demilitarised Zone in North Korea in June 2019.
The meetings came after Trump initially mocked Kim as "rocket man" during a speech in 2017.
The US president said in August that he expected to meet later this year with Kim, hoping to revive the bond he claims to have forged with the leader of nuclear-armed North Korea in his first term.

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.
Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.
Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.
A New York Times story , external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.
Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.
"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.
In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.
Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.
"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.
A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.
The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including US president Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”
However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.
Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin sanctioned a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before launching a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.
The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.
Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.
Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.
The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.
The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.
Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.
“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”
The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”
“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

Venâncio Mondlane was the runner-up in the 2024 presidential election
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
Mondlane arrived at the Supreme Court early on Tuesday with "great peace of mind", and was greeted by dozens of supporters.
"As you can see, I arrive calm, confident in the work of my legal team," he told journalists gathered outside court, amid a heavy police presence.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.
Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.
European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.
About 96 people died during the 2024 protests, according to police
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.
In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own
Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, have been sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.
The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – were sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.
Before the parliamentary session, Student List supporters gathered outside the National Assembly to cheer their representatives. Some of them performed the traditional kolo circle dance in celebration.
Meanwhile, there were jeers and whistles for arrivals from Vučić’s party. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over the head of the SNS candidate Lidija Vukićević.
A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.
Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”
Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”
The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.
El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.
She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.
Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.
Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.
That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.
After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.
Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.
“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”
In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital Manama on Tuesday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they launched a drone attack, the third in five days after a weeks-long lull.
Bahrain's armed forces intercepted "Iranian aerial attacks in the kingdom's skies", according to state television, while Iran's Guards said they targeted a US-operated radar system.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry, in a post on X, warned of a "possible threat" and called on the country's residents to remain calm, move to the nearest safe place and follow only official sources for information on developments.
Bahraini officials also said the country's air defence systems had intercepted attacks from Iran.
No confirmed report has yet been released on any impact of Iranian drones on the radar system at Sheikh Isa base or on the extent of any possible damage.
The public relations arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps described the pre-dawn attack on Tuesday as a response to what it called "the continued violation of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran" by US military drones.
It said the operation formed part of ongoing air-defence and electronic warfare measures to track, destroy and capture US drones of the MQ and MQM-170 series.
"Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the Guards' Sepah news website said.
The Guards also warned that continued use of regional bases and military facilities for actions against Iran would not go unanswered.
Bahrain was heavily targeted earlier in the war, which started in February, but had been peaceful for weeks until an Iranian drone attack on Friday. A second followed on Sunday.
Friday's strike was the first Iranian attack against a Gulf country since early September.
The US military said it had shot down two drones launched Friday by Iranian forces, while the Bahraini army said it had intercepted Sunday's attack.
Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has experienced numerous Iranian attacks since US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered the Middle East war in February.
Since September, the conflict has mainly been restricted to the area around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Tehran attempting to control the oil shipping route.
The Middle East war will be on the agenda during an unprecedented trilateral summit between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, scheduled this week in China, according to the White House.
As talks aimed at ending the war appear to be deadlocked, a third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is operating in the Middle East, the US military said on Monday.

Venancio Mondlane faces five charges, the most serious being instigating ‘terrorism’.
Mozambique’s opposition leader has arrived at the country’s Supreme Court to stand trial over his alleged role in deadly protests that followed 2024’s disputed election results .
Venancio Mondlane addressed reporters outside the court in Maputo on Tuesday. He faces five charges, the most serious of which is instigating “terrorism”. If found guilty, he could be jailed for up to 24 years.
“I arrive calm and confident in my legal team,” Mondlane said.
Months of antigovernment protests broke out in Mozambique in 2024 after Mondlane came second in national elections. President Daniel Chapo and his Frelimo party beat Mondlane, extending Frelimo’s time in power to more than 50 years. Mondlane disputes the results, and his allegations of harassment of the opposition have been echoed by rights groups, including Human Rights Watch.
Following the elections in 2024, the organisation said the vote had been marred by political killings, widespread irregularities, and restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. Frelimo denies any wrongdoing.
Amnesty International says more than 300 people were killed during protests against the election results. It accused authorities of waging a crackdown against demonstrators, with police allegedly using unlawful force, mass arbitrary arrests and suppression of information.
Mondlane has also been charged with inciting “terrorism”, advocacy of crime, public incitement to a crime, and incitement of civil disobedience.
Thousands of people gathered for protests in response to calls by Mondlane to organise against the results. While preparing to challenge the vote, Mondlane’s lawyer and aide were shot dead.
Before Tuesday’s trial, Mondlane accused the government of attempting to silence him during a livestream on Facebook.
“The message being sent is that you must remain silent. You must remain in captivity, in prison, in darkness,” he said.
“In truth, Venancio is being used as an example to an entire generation: A warning that nobody should dare to rise up against the regime, against an empire of kleptocracy, or against the system of oppression that we have lived under for 50 years.”

Brazil’s star forward scored a 12-minute hat-trick in the record world champions’ thumping of the hosts in a friendly.
Vinicius Junior hit a 12-minute hat-trick in the first half as Brazil turned on the style in a 7-0 trouncing of Singapore in an international friendly.
Endrick, Estevao, Rayan and substitute Allan also found the net as the South Americans brushed aside their hosts with a dominant performance at the National Stadium on Tuesday.
Brazil were much changed from their 3-2 loss to Japan on Saturday , in which manager Carlo Ancelotti and captain Raphinha were shown red cards, with Vinicius one of only four players retaining their places in the starting lineup.
Bruno Guimaraes took over as skipper and set up the opener after nine minutes, playing a quick pass to Vinicius, who wrong-footed Singapore captain Hariss Harun with his first touch before dispatching a left-footed shot past goalkeeper Izwan Mahbud.
The Real Madrid forward notched his second in the 15th minute after a quick counterattack by the Selecao as Endrick laid the ball off for his unmarked teammate to slot home.
Vinicius was denied by Izwan shortly afterwards, but he completed his hat-trick in the 21st minute when he was found completely unmarked in the six-yard box by Estevao’s low centre.
Rayan had an effort disallowed for offside, but Endrick added to Brazil’s lead in the 31st minute with a low effort from range that found the bottom right corner.
Estevao also had a goal disallowed for a foul by Vinicius, but the Chelsea winger added to Brazil’s tally just after the interval with a deflected shot from the edge of the box.
Rayan rocked the crossbar soon after, but the endeavour of the Bournemouth forward was rewarded in the 65th minute when he rounded substitute goalkeeper Syazwan Buhari to make it 6-0.
Brazil rang the changes in the closing stages, and Allan came off the bench to grab the seventh goal in the 74th minute with a low-angled shot that nicked off Raoul Suhaimi on its way into the net.

Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
The leaders of China , the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any major breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine .
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran .
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

Protesters hurl bricks, torch vehicles and block the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district, Mymensingh.
Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.
Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district of Mymensingh.
Bangladesh is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for big international brands, including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.
But growing worker unrest over wages, which began last month, has disrupted the industry that generates $38bn annually and employs more than four million people.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) – a 140-percent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.
About 500 of the country’s 4,500 garment factories are shut, sources told the AFP news agency, further stoking unrest among workers.
A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.
“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” one worker, Khanom, 24, told AFP.
Tensions were also running high in the garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on Dhaka’s outskirts.
The wage board , comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.
The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January next year.
“We want to return to our machines,” garment worker Rakib, 28, told AFP.
“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.
Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning, but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.
In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.
A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a BGMEA source told AFP.
The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.
In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.
“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.
The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

Shares in Deutsche Bank plunged Tuesday after international media outlets published reports detailing the bank's questionable business practices over the past 20 years, including its ties to Russian oligarchs, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump before he became the US president.
Dubbed " Inside Deutsche Bank ", the investigation was conducted by more than 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.
Shared by unidentified whistleblowers and based on millions of emails and other documents, it outlines the bank's business over the past 20 years, including its ties to Russian oligarchs, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump before he became the US president in 2017. The data originated from two whistleblowers and was channelled through South African and Indian journalists to more than 50 media outlets worldwide.
According to the reports, the bank at times prioritised commercial interests over compliance with international sanctions, anti-money laundering regulations and even its own internal procedures.
German police searched the bank's Frankfurt headquarters and its Berlin office offices in January this year as part of a money-laundering probe .
Read more German police search Deutsche Bank offices in money-laundering probe
The documents reportedly also detail how Deutsche Bank courted oligarchs and sought to expand its Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine , despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
The reports also note that the bank's announced withdrawal from the Russian market after the Ukraine invasion remains incomplete.
As of last year, Deutsche Bank still employed 162 people in the country and its local subsidiary generated a pre-tax profit of €61 million ($67 million).
The leaks raised questions about internal controls and practices at Germany's largest bank and reignited questions regarding chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution. Deutsche Bank shares fell by nearly 6 percent shortly after the opening of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
Documents cited by the media outlets indicate that Sewing was among the participants in the working group that developed the Russia strategy.
The documents indicate that Deutsche Bank set up controversial tax-optimisation schemes for wealthy clients and contain new details regarding its long-standing business relationships with Epstein as well as Trump.
In 2023, Deutsche Bank agreed to pay $75 million to settle a lawsuit accusing it of benefitting from Epstein's sex-trafficking business.
In 2021 it reportedly cut ties with Trump in the wake of the January 6 riot on the US Capitol building
The data also suggests that criminal networks were able to funnel money through the bank.
Read more Deutsche Bank settles Epstein sex-trafficking abuse lawsuit for $75 million
It offered insights into arms deals involving problematic states, the bank's support for clients in environmentally damaging industries and holding donation accounts for Germany's far-right AfD political party , despite internal opposition.
Deutsche Bank does not dispute that the records are genuine, though it refers to them as "purported internal documents" and noted that some of the incidents cited date back more than two decades.
The bank said that it reviewed these matters with regulatory authorities at the time and that it had invested €7 billion between 2019 and 2025 to strengthen its control systems.
It is now "a different bank", it said, pointing to record profits in 2025 and progress made on compliance.

Mohamed Hadid ise daha önce iki kez evlendi. Mary Butler ile yaptığı ilk evliliğinden üç kızı dünyaya geldi. Gigi ve Bella Hadid 'in annesi olan Hollandalı model Yolanda Hadid ile evliliğinden ise kızlarının yanı sıra Anwar adında bir de oğlu dünyaya geldi.

Benim için her zaman önemli olan, bu jestlerin ardındaki samimiyet olmuştur" ifadesini kullandı.
Silva, "Bazen hayattaki en güzel anlar, dilediğinizi bile bilmediğiniz anlardır" diye ekledi.

Gigi ve Bella Hadid kardeşler, üvey kardeşleri Aydan Nix ile 2023'te tanıştıklarını 2025'te açıkladı.

Vogue Arabia'ya konuşan Mohamed Hadid, nişanlısının inanılmaz derecede ilgili, sevgi dolu ve sadık kişiliğine hayran olduğunu söyledi.

Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.
Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.
The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.
The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade , to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.
Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.
According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.
The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.
The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.
The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.
A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.
Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

Ezgi Mola ile Mustafa Aksakallı'nın evliliği ve ayrılık süreci yeniden gündeme geldi. 2025 yılında boşanan çift hakkında ortaya atılan aldatma iddialarına yanıt veren Mola, eski eşini savunarak Mustafa Aksakallı'nın “dünyanın en iyi kalpli insanlarından biri” olduğunu söyledi. Ünlü oyuncu, ayrılık nedenini ise Bertolt Brecht'in “Madem İyisin” şiirinden yola çıkarak anlattı. Peki, Ezgi Mola boşandı mı? Mustafa Aksakallı ve Ezgi Mola ayrıldı mı, neden boşandılar? Detaylar...
Oyuncu Ezgi Mola ile Mustafa Aksakallı, 8 Mayıs 2023 tarihinde evlendi. Çift, Haziran 2025'te ayrılık kararını duyurdu. Ayrılık açıklamasının ardından sosyal medyada çeşitli yorumlar yapılırken, Mola son olarak konuk olduğu Ritmini Bul Talk Show programında boşanma sürecine ilişkin değerlendirmelerde bulundu.
Evet. Ezgi Mola ve Mustafa Aksakallı, Haziran 2025'te ayrılık kararlarını açıkladı. Mola, ayrılık sürecinde ortak bir karar aldıklarını ve dostluklarını korumak istediklerini belirtmişti. Oyuncunun son açıklamaları da çiftin evliliklerini sonlandırırken arkadaşlıklarını sürdürme isteğine işaret etti.
Ezgi Mola, boşanma kararının ardından gündeme gelen aldatma iddialarını reddetti. Sosyal medyada eski eşinin kendisini aldattığı yönünde yapılan yorumları hatırlatan oyuncu, bu iddialara tepki göstererek Mustafa Aksakallı'nın çok iyi kalpli biri olduğunu söyledi.
Mola, Ritmini Bul Talk Show'da yaptığı açıklamada, “Mustafa gerçekten dünyanın en iyi kalpli insanlarından biri. Onun hakkını yiyemem” ifadelerini kullandı. Oyuncu, ayrılığın ardından bu kez de neden boşandıklarının sorgulandığını belirterek, bir insanın iyi kalpli olmasıyla iki kişinin ilişkiyi sürdürebilmesinin aynı şey olmadığını dile getirdi.
Ayrılık nedenini anlatırken Alman yazar Bertolt Brecht'in “Madem İyisin” adlı şiirine değinen Ezgi Mola, ilişkilerde yalnızca iyi kalpli olmanın yeterli olmadığını vurguladı. Oyuncu, “Herkes iyi olabilir ama önemli olan senin bana iyi gelip gelmediğin” sözleriyle ilişkilerde karşılıklı uyumun önemine dikkat çekti.
Mola, düşüncesini “Senin iyiliğin bana iyi geliyor mu, ben de sana iyi geliyor muyum?” sözleriyle açıkladı. İyi bir ilişki kurabilmenin, gerektiğinde ayrılabilmeyi de kapsadığını belirten oyuncu, “Zaten ayrılabiliyorsan iyi bir ilişki kurmuşsun demektir” dedi.
